stem: Rural development refers to:
options: Actions and measures to improve the economic and social life of the people in the rural (village) areas
solution: Rural development refers to the actions, processes, and measures aimed at improving the economic and social life (the standard of living and well-being) of the people living in the rural (village) areas. Since a large majority of India's population lives in villages and depends on agriculture, rural development is crucial for the country's overall progress. It involves improving many areas — agriculture and allied activities, rural infrastructure (roads, electricity, water), credit and marketing, education and health, poverty alleviation, and employment — in the villages. Understanding what rural development means is a key prelims point. Rural development is the set of measures to improve the economic and social life of the people in the rural (village) areas.

stem: Rural development in India is important mainly because:
options: a very large proportion of India's population lives in villages and depends on agriculture
it is required by other countries
solution: Rural development in India is especially important because a very large proportion of India's population (well over half, historically about two-thirds or more) lives in the rural (village) areas and depends on agriculture and allied activities for their livelihood. Since so much of the country's population and workforce is rural, India cannot develop or reduce its poverty without developing its villages — improving rural incomes, agriculture, infrastructure, and social conditions. Neglecting the rural areas would leave the majority of Indians behind. So rural development is central to India's overall development and to reducing poverty. Understanding why rural development matters (most Indians are rural) is a prelims point. Rural development is important because a very large share of India's population lives in villages and depends on agriculture.

stem: Key areas that require fresh initiatives for rural development include the development of human resources, land reforms, infrastructure, and:
options: credit and marketing facilities, and measures to alleviate poverty (and bring about employment)
solution: The key areas that require fresh initiatives/emphasis for rural development include: the development of human resources (literacy — especially female literacy, education, skills, and health, including sanitation and public health); land reforms; the development of productive resources in each locality; infrastructure development (electricity, irrigation, roads, transport, banking, marketing, agricultural research, and IT); special measures for the alleviation of poverty and to improve the living conditions of the weaker sections (with access to productive resources); and the provision of credit and marketing facilities for farmers. Together, action in these areas is needed to develop the rural areas. Understanding these key areas of rural development is a prelims point. Rural development requires initiatives in human resources, land reforms, infrastructure, credit and marketing, and poverty alleviation.

stem: Rural credit (loans for farmers) is important because farmers often need money for inputs and to bridge the gap between __________.
options: sowing the crop and harvesting/selling it (when they have income)
solution: Rural credit (loans/finance for farmers) is very important because farming has a long time gap between the sowing of a crop (when the farmer must spend money on inputs — seeds, fertilisers, labour, etc.) and the harvesting and selling of the crop (when the farmer finally earns income from it). During this gap, the farmer has expenses but no income, and so needs credit (loans) to meet the costs of cultivation (and often for consumption/family needs too, and for buying land or equipment). Adequate, timely, and cheap credit is therefore essential for farmers to carry on and improve their farming. (The lack of it forces them to borrow from moneylenders at very high interest.) Understanding why rural credit is needed (to bridge the sowing-to-harvest gap) is a prelims point. Rural credit is important because farmers need money to bridge the long gap between sowing the crop and harvesting/selling it.

stem: Before institutional (bank) credit spread, farmers were largely dependent for loans on __________, who charged very high interest rates and exploited them.
solution: Before institutional (organised) credit — from banks, cooperatives, etc. — spread in the rural areas, farmers were largely dependent for their loans on the informal, non-institutional lenders — chiefly the village moneylenders (mahajans/sahukars), and also traders and landlords. These moneylenders exploited the farmers: they charged very high (usurious) rates of interest, manipulated the accounts, and kept the farmers in perpetual debt (debt-trap), often ending up taking over the farmers' land. To free the farmers from this exploitation, the government promoted the spread of institutional credit (cooperatives, banks) to the rural areas. Understanding the earlier dependence on exploitative moneylenders is a prelims point. Before institutional credit spread, farmers depended on moneylenders, who charged very high interest and exploited them.

stem: A major step to provide institutional credit to farmers and reduce their dependence on moneylenders was the __________ of banks in 1969.
solution: A major step to provide institutional credit to the rural areas (farmers) and to reduce their dependence on the exploitative moneylenders was the nationalisation of banks in 1969 (when 14 major commercial banks were nationalised — taken over by the government; and more in 1980). After nationalisation, the banks were directed to expand their branches into the rural areas and to provide credit to agriculture and other priority sectors (like small industries and weaker sections) at reasonable rates. This 'social banking' greatly expanded institutional credit to farmers. Understanding that bank nationalisation (1969) aimed to spread rural/priority credit is a prelims-relevant point. The nationalisation of banks in 1969 was a major step to provide institutional credit to farmers and reduce their dependence on moneylenders.

stem: The apex (top) bank that coordinates and refinances rural credit (agricultural and rural development finance) in India is:
options: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development)
solution: NABARD — the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (set up in 1982) — is the apex (top-level) institution that coordinates, oversees, and refinances the rural credit system in India. It provides refinance (funds) to, and supervises, the other rural credit institutions (cooperative banks, regional rural banks, and commercial banks' rural lending), and it promotes agricultural and rural development (financing infrastructure, and supporting programmes like self-help groups). So NABARD sits at the top of the rural/agricultural credit structure. Understanding NABARD (apex rural credit bank) is a prelims-relevant point. NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) is the apex institution coordinating and refinancing rural credit in India.

stem: Small groups of (usually poor, rural) people, especially women, who pool their small savings and give loans to members (promoting savings and micro-credit) are called:
solution: Self-Help Groups (SHGs) are small groups of people — usually poor, and often women — from the rural (or urban poor) areas, who come together voluntarily to pool their small savings regularly into a common fund, from which they give small loans (micro-credit) to their members (in times of need), at reasonable interest. SHGs promote thrift (saving) and provide credit to the poor (who cannot easily get bank loans, lacking collateral), and they empower members (especially women) economically and socially. They are often linked to banks (which lend to the group). SHGs (and 'microfinance') have become an important tool of rural development and poverty alleviation. Understanding Self-Help Groups (SHGs) is a prelims-relevant point. Self-Help Groups (SHGs) are small groups (often of women) who pool savings and give micro-loans to members, promoting savings and credit.

stem: The lending of very small loans to the poor (who lack collateral and cannot access normal banks), often through SHGs, is called:
solution: Micro-credit (or microfinance) is the provision of very small loans (and other basic financial services) to the poor — people who are too poor to access the normal banking system (they lack collateral/security and a credit history). This micro-credit is often provided through Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and specialised microfinance institutions. By giving the poor access to small loans, microfinance helps them to start or run small income-generating activities (petty businesses, farming, crafts), meet emergencies, and escape the clutches of moneylenders — thus helping to reduce poverty and empower the poor (especially women). Understanding micro-credit/microfinance is a prelims-relevant point. Micro-credit (microfinance) is the lending of very small loans to the poor (who lack collateral), often through SHGs.

stem: Agricultural marketing refers to the process of:
options: gathering, storing, grading, transporting, and selling the farm produce — getting it from the farmer to the consumer
solution: Agricultural marketing refers to the whole process of moving the farm produce from the farmer (producer) to the final consumer — including the various activities and services involved: the gathering/assembling of the produce, its storage (warehousing), grading (sorting by quality) and processing, transportation, and finally its sale/distribution through the markets. Efficient agricultural marketing is important so that farmers get a fair price for their produce, wastage is minimised, and consumers get the produce at reasonable prices. (Poor marketing — with too many middlemen, poor storage, and manipulation — hurts the farmers.) Understanding agricultural marketing is a prelims point. Agricultural marketing is the process of gathering, storing, grading, transporting, and selling the farm produce from the farmer to the consumer.

stem: A problem in agricultural marketing that hurts farmers is the presence of too many __________ (middlemen), who take a large share of the price.
solution: A major problem in agricultural marketing (especially the traditional/unregulated system) that hurts farmers is the presence of too many intermediaries (middlemen) — the chain of traders, commission agents, wholesalers, and retailers between the farmer and the consumer. Each of these middlemen takes a cut/margin, so a large share of the price finally paid by the consumer goes to the intermediaries, while the farmer (the actual producer) receives only a small fraction of it. The farmers are often at a disadvantage (lacking information, storage, and bargaining power, and in debt to the traders), so they get low prices. Reducing the number of intermediaries and improving marketing helps farmers get a fairer share. Understanding the problem of too many middlemen is a prelims point. Too many intermediaries (middlemen) in agricultural marketing take a large share of the price, leaving the farmer with only a small fraction.

stem: To improve agricultural marketing and protect farmers, the government set up regulated markets (mandis), provided warehousing, and introduced the __________ to guarantee farmers a fair price.
solution: To improve agricultural marketing and protect the farmers, the government took several measures, including: setting up regulated markets (mandis) — organised markets where sales are supervised/regulated to ensure fair dealings and prevent the cheating of farmers; providing infrastructure like warehousing/storage (so farmers can store produce and avoid distress sales) and grading; and introducing the Minimum Support Price (MSP) — a guaranteed minimum price at which the government will buy certain crops, so that farmers are assured of a fair/remunerative price and protected from a sharp fall in prices. Along with cooperative marketing (farmers' cooperatives selling produce), these measures aim to give farmers a fairer deal. Understanding these marketing-improvement measures (regulated markets, MSP, etc.) is a prelims point. The government set up regulated markets, warehousing, and the Minimum Support Price (MSP) to improve marketing and guarantee farmers a fair price.

stem: Diversification of agriculture — into activities beyond growing food-grain crops — is important because it:
options: provides farmers with additional/alternative sources of income and employment (reducing risk and dependence on one crop)
solution: Diversification of agriculture — expanding into a wider range of crops and, especially, into 'allied' and non-farm activities beyond the growing of the main food-grain crops — is important because it provides farmers with additional and alternative sources of income and employment. This: reduces their dependence on (and the risk from) a single crop (if one crop fails or its price falls, they have other sources); makes fuller and more productive use of the labour and land (including in the off-season); and can raise incomes. Diversification includes shifting some land to other crops, and — importantly — moving into non-crop allied activities (like animal husbandry/dairy, fisheries, and horticulture) and non-farm employment (like agro-processing, services). Understanding the importance of agricultural diversification (income, employment, reduced risk) is a prelims point. Diversification of agriculture gives farmers additional/alternative income and employment, reducing their risk and dependence on one crop.

stem: The 'allied' activities that are an important part of agricultural diversification and rural livelihoods include animal husbandry (dairy/livestock), fisheries, and:
solution: The 'allied' activities — the non-crop activities related to agriculture that are an important part of diversification and rural livelihoods — include: animal husbandry (livestock rearing, especially dairying — keeping cattle/buffaloes for milk — and poultry, etc.); fisheries (fish farming and fishing); and horticulture (the growing of fruits, vegetables, flowers, and plantation crops). These allied activities provide important additional sources of income, employment, and nutrition for rural households (often for the small/marginal farmers and the landless), and they help diversify and strengthen the rural economy. (For example, dairying was transformed by the White Revolution/Operation Flood.) Understanding the allied activities (animal husbandry, fisheries, horticulture) is a prelims point. Allied activities of agriculture include animal husbandry (dairy/livestock), fisheries, and horticulture (fruits, vegetables, flowers).

stem: The 'White Revolution' (Operation Flood) transformed which allied activity into a major source of rural income (making India the largest milk producer)?
solution: The 'White Revolution' (Operation Flood) transformed dairying (milk production) into a major source of rural income and made India the largest producer of milk in the world. Through a nationwide network of dairy cooperatives (the model pioneered by Amul in Gujarat, led by Verghese Kurien), milk from millions of small rural producers was collected, processed, and marketed efficiently — greatly increasing milk production and giving stable incomes to a huge number of rural (often poor) households (and women). The White Revolution is a success story of diversification into an allied activity (dairying) and of the cooperative model in rural development. Understanding the White Revolution's transformation of dairying is a prelims point. The White Revolution (Operation Flood) transformed dairying (milk production) into a major source of rural income, making India the largest milk producer.

stem: Organic farming (a growing form of sustainable agriculture) is a system that:
options: uses lots of chemical fertilisers and pesticides
avoids chemical fertilisers and pesticides, relying instead on natural/organic inputs (manure, bio-fertilisers, natural pest control)
solution: Organic farming is a system/method of agriculture that avoids (or minimises) the use of synthetic chemical fertilisers, chemical pesticides, and other artificial chemicals, relying instead on natural and organic inputs and methods — such as organic manure (compost, farmyard manure), bio-fertilisers, crop rotation, green manure, and natural/biological methods of pest control. Organic farming is a form of sustainable agriculture: it is more environmentally friendly (it protects the soil, water, and ecology, and avoids chemical pollution), produces healthier, chemical-free food, and can be sustainable in the long run. It is being promoted as an alternative to the chemical-intensive farming of the Green Revolution (which caused environmental problems). Understanding organic farming (chemical-free, natural, sustainable) is a prelims-relevant point. Organic farming avoids chemical fertilisers and pesticides, relying on natural/organic inputs — a sustainable, eco-friendly method.

stem: The programme that provides a legal guarantee of 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households (whose adults want unskilled manual work) is:
options: MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act)
solution: MGNREGA — the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (2005) — is the landmark programme that provides a legal guarantee of up to 100 days of wage employment per year to every rural household whose adult members are willing to do unskilled manual work. It aims to provide livelihood security to the rural poor (guaranteeing them work and income), especially in the lean/off-agricultural seasons, and the work done also creates useful rural assets/infrastructure (roads, water conservation, etc.). MGNREGA is one of the world's largest employment/social-security programmes and a major instrument of rural poverty alleviation and rural development. Understanding MGNREGA (the rural employment guarantee) is a prelims-relevant point. MGNREGA guarantees up to 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households wanting unskilled manual work.

stem: The 'cooperative' model (where members join together to run an enterprise for their mutual benefit) has been successfully used in rural India especially in:
options: dairy (milk) — as in Amul — and in credit and marketing
solution: The cooperative model — in which the members (e.g., farmers or rural producers) join together to collectively own and run an enterprise for their mutual benefit (sharing the work and the profits) — has been successfully used in rural India especially in dairying (the milk cooperatives, most famously the Amul cooperative in Gujarat, which was the model for the White Revolution), and also in agricultural credit (cooperative credit societies/banks) and in the marketing and processing of farm produce (marketing and processing cooperatives — e.g., for sugar). Cooperatives empower the small rural producers by giving them collective strength (in getting credit, inputs, fair prices, and markets), and they are an important part of rural development. Understanding the success of cooperatives in dairy/credit/marketing is a prelims-relevant point. The cooperative model has been very successful in rural India in dairy (Amul) and in credit and marketing.

stem: Non-farm employment (jobs outside agriculture, in the rural areas) is important because:
options: agriculture cannot provide enough jobs/income for all rural people, so non-farm work (in agro-processing, services, crafts, etc.) provides additional livelihoods and reduces dependence on agriculture
it forces people out of villages
solution: Non-farm employment — jobs and livelihoods outside crop agriculture, within the rural areas (such as in agro-processing and agri-business, small industries and handicrafts, trade and shops, transport, construction, and various services, and IT-enabled services) — is important because agriculture alone cannot provide enough jobs and income for all the rural people (the land is limited and overcrowded, and much rural labour is under-employed/seasonal). Developing non-farm employment provides additional and alternative sources of livelihood and income for rural households (including the landless and the small farmers, and in the agricultural off-season), reduces the excessive dependence on and pressure on agriculture, and helps diversify and strengthen the rural economy — reducing rural poverty and slowing distress migration to cities. Understanding the importance of non-farm employment is a prelims point. Non-farm employment is important because agriculture can't provide enough jobs/income for all rural people, so it provides additional livelihoods and reduces dependence on agriculture.

stem: Assertion (A): Providing adequate and cheap institutional credit is important for rural development. Reason (R): It frees farmers from exploitation by moneylenders and enables them to invest in and improve their farming. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that providing adequate, timely, and cheap institutional credit is important for rural development. And the reason is (R) that such credit frees the farmers from exploitation by the moneylenders (who charged very high interest and kept them in a debt-trap), and it enables the farmers to invest in and improve their farming — to buy better seeds, fertilisers, equipment, and irrigation, and to adopt modern methods (as the Green Revolution required) and diversify — thereby raising their productivity and income. So, by rescuing farmers from usurious moneylenders and empowering them to invest, institutional credit promotes rural development — R correctly explains A. Understanding the importance of institutional rural credit is a prelims point. Institutional credit is important for rural development because it frees farmers from moneylenders and lets them invest in and improve their farming.

stem: The rapid growth of the horticulture sector (fruits, vegetables, flowers), an important form of agricultural diversification, is called the __________ Revolution.
solution: The rapid growth and development of the horticulture sector — the production of fruits, vegetables, flowers (floriculture), and other such crops — is called the 'Golden Revolution' (the period of golden revolution in horticulture). Horticulture is an important form of agricultural diversification: it provides higher incomes to farmers (horticultural crops are often more valuable than food grains), improves nutrition, and generates employment (it is labour-intensive). India has become a major producer of fruits and vegetables. (For reference among the 'colour revolutions': Green — food grains; White — milk; Blue — fisheries; Yellow — oilseeds; Golden — horticulture/honey.) Understanding the Golden Revolution (horticulture) is a prelims point. The rapid growth of horticulture (fruits, vegetables, flowers) is called the Golden Revolution.

stem: The 'Blue Revolution' in India refers to the rapid development of:
solution: The 'Blue Revolution' refers to the rapid development and growth of the fisheries sector — the production of fish and other aquatic products (from both inland/freshwater fisheries and aquaculture, and marine/sea fisheries). Fisheries are an important allied activity and a source of income, employment, food, and export earnings, especially for the fishing communities and for people in the coastal and riverine areas. The Blue Revolution boosted fish production and India's fisheries. (For reference: Green → food grains; White → milk; Blue → fish; Yellow → oilseeds.) Understanding that the Blue Revolution is about fisheries is a prelims point. The 'Blue Revolution' refers to the rapid development of the fisheries (fish production) sector.

stem: The 'Yellow Revolution' refers to a large increase in the production of:
solution: The 'Yellow Revolution' refers to the large increase in the production of oilseeds (and hence edible oils) in India (the yellow colour referring to oilseeds like mustard, and to cooking oil). It was aimed at making India more self-sufficient in edible oils (reducing costly imports). (For reference among the 'colour revolutions': Green → food grains; White → milk; Blue → fish; Yellow → oilseeds; Golden → horticulture.) Understanding that the Yellow Revolution is about oilseeds is a prelims point. The 'Yellow Revolution' refers to the increase in the production of oilseeds (edible oils).

stem: The rearing of silkworms to produce silk (an income-generating rural activity) is called:
solution: Sericulture is the rearing of silkworms (on mulberry or other leaves) to produce silk — the raising of silkworms and the production of raw silk from their cocoons. It is an important income-generating, labour-intensive rural activity (and a form of agricultural diversification), providing employment and income to many rural households (India is a major silk producer). (For reference: apiculture = bee-keeping/honey; pisciculture = fish farming; horticulture = fruits/vegetables/flowers.) Understanding sericulture (silkworm rearing for silk) is a prelims point. Sericulture is the rearing of silkworms to produce silk, an income-generating rural activity.

stem: The keeping of honey bees (for honey and wax), a supplementary source of rural income, is called:
solution: Apiculture is the keeping/rearing of honey bees — bee-keeping — for the production of honey and beeswax (and for the pollination of crops). It is a supplementary, low-cost source of income and employment for rural households (and a form of diversification), and it also benefits agriculture (bees pollinate crops, improving yields). (For reference: sericulture = silkworm rearing; aquaculture = fish/aquatic farming; poultry = raising birds like chickens.) Understanding apiculture (bee-keeping) is a prelims point. Apiculture is the keeping of honey bees for honey and wax, a supplementary source of rural income.

stem: The 'electronic National Agriculture Market' — an online trading platform launched to help farmers get better prices by connecting mandis across the country — is called:
solution: e-NAM (electronic National Agriculture Market) is an online (electronic) trading platform launched by the government to create a unified national market for agricultural produce. It connects the agricultural markets (mandis) across the country onto a single online platform, so that farmers can sell their produce to buyers anywhere (not just the local mandi), through transparent online bidding — helping them get better and more competitive prices, reducing the role of middlemen, and improving marketing efficiency. e-NAM is a modern initiative to reform agricultural marketing. Understanding e-NAM (the online national agriculture market) is a prelims-relevant point. e-NAM (electronic National Agriculture Market) is an online platform connecting mandis across India to help farmers get better prices.

stem: A system in which a farmer agrees, in advance, to produce a specified crop (of a certain quality and quantity) for a buyer/company (at a pre-agreed price) is called:
solution: Contract farming is a system in which a farmer enters into an agreement (contract), in advance (before the growing season), with a buyer — such as an agri-business company, a processor, or an exporter — to produce a specified crop (of a certain quality and quantity) and to sell it to that buyer at a pre-agreed price. The buyer often also provides inputs (seeds, technology, guidance). Contract farming can benefit the farmer by assuring a market and a price in advance (reducing price risk and marketing problems) and giving access to inputs/technology; but it can also have risks (dependence on the company, unfair contracts). It is one of the alternative/modern marketing arrangements. Understanding contract farming is a prelims-relevant point. Contract farming is where a farmer agrees in advance to produce a specified crop for a buyer at a pre-agreed price.

stem: Alternative marketing channels in which farmers sell their produce DIRECTLY to consumers (removing the middlemen) include Apni Mandi (Punjab/Haryana) and __________ (Andhra Pradesh).
solution: Alternative marketing channels have been developed in which farmers sell their produce directly to the consumers (bypassing the many middlemen), so that farmers get a better price and consumers get fresher produce at a lower price. Examples include: 'Apni Mandi' (in Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan); 'Rythu Bazars' (farmers' markets, for vegetables and fruits, in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana); 'Hadaspar Mandi' (Pune); and 'Uzhavar Sandhais' (in Tamil Nadu). These direct farmer-to-consumer markets are examples of improving agricultural marketing to benefit farmers. Understanding these alternative direct-marketing channels (like Rythu Bazars) is a prelims-relevant point. Rythu Bazars (Andhra Pradesh) and Apni Mandi are alternative markets where farmers sell directly to consumers, removing middlemen.

stem: Cooperative marketing (farmers selling their produce jointly through a cooperative) helps farmers by:
options: giving them collective/greater bargaining strength to get a fair price (and to store, process, and transport produce together)
solution: Cooperative marketing — where the farmers of an area join together to form a marketing cooperative and sell their produce jointly (collectively) through it — helps the farmers by: giving them greater collective bargaining strength/power (as a group, they can negotiate better, fairer prices than an individual small farmer could) and reducing their exploitation by traders/middlemen; and enabling them to jointly arrange storage, grading, processing, transport, and marketing (achieving economies of scale and better facilities). By pooling their produce and marketing it together, small farmers overcome their individual weakness and get a fairer share of the price. (Cooperative marketing has been successful, e.g., in sugar, milk, and cotton.) Understanding the benefits of cooperative marketing is a prelims point. Cooperative marketing gives farmers greater collective bargaining strength for a fair price, and helps them store, process, and transport produce together.

stem: The government's road-building programme to connect all rural villages/habitations with all-weather roads (improving rural infrastructure) is the:
solution: The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) is the government's rural roads programme, aimed at providing all-weather road connectivity to all unconnected rural villages/habitations. Good roads are crucial rural infrastructure: they connect villages to markets (so farmers can sell their produce and get inputs), to towns, schools, hospitals, and jobs, and they promote trade, mobility, and development. So PMGSY (rural road connectivity) is an important part of rural infrastructure development. (The 'Golden Quadrilateral' is a separate programme connecting the major cities by highways.) Understanding PMGSY (rural roads) is a prelims-relevant point. The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) is the programme to connect all rural villages with all-weather roads.

stem: A special credit facility that gives farmers a simple, flexible way to borrow (a card-based limit for their cultivation needs) is the:
solution: The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) is a special credit facility/scheme that gives farmers a simple, timely, and flexible way to obtain credit for their agricultural (cultivation) needs. Under the scheme, a farmer is given a credit card with a sanctioned credit limit (based on the farming needs), from which they can draw money (loans) as and when needed for buying inputs (seeds, fertilisers, etc.) and other cultivation expenses, and repay after the harvest — without the hassle of applying for a fresh loan each time. The Kisan Credit Card thus makes institutional credit more accessible and convenient for farmers, reducing their dependence on moneylenders. Understanding the Kisan Credit Card is a prelims-relevant point. The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) gives farmers a simple, flexible card-based credit limit for their cultivation needs.

stem: The multi-agency approach to rural (agricultural) credit in India involves cooperatives, commercial banks, and __________ (banks set up specially to serve the rural areas).
solution: India follows a 'multi-agency approach' to rural/agricultural credit — providing institutional credit to the rural areas through several types of institutions together: the cooperative credit societies/banks (a three-tier structure of primary, district, and state cooperative banks); the commercial banks (especially after their nationalisation, directed to lend to agriculture/priority sectors); and the Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) — banks set up specially (from 1975) to serve the rural areas and provide credit to farmers, agricultural labourers, and rural artisans and small entrepreneurs. All these are refinanced and coordinated at the top by NABARD. So RRBs are the specialised rural banks in this multi-agency system. Understanding the multi-agency rural credit system (including RRBs) is a prelims-relevant point. India's rural credit comes from cooperatives, commercial banks, and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), coordinated by NABARD.

stem: The lowest/primary tier of the cooperative credit structure, which directly deals with the farmers in the village, is the:
solution: The Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS) is the lowest/primary tier (the base) of the three-tier short-term cooperative credit structure, and it is the unit that directly deals with the individual farmers at the village level — it is the village-level cooperative society that collects deposits from and gives loans (credit) to the farmer-members for their agricultural needs. Above the PACS are the District Central Cooperative Banks (at the district level) and the State Cooperative Bank (at the state/apex level). So the PACS is the grassroots cooperative that provides credit directly to the village farmers. Understanding the PACS (primary cooperative credit society) is a prelims-relevant point. The Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS) is the village-level base of the cooperative credit structure that deals directly with farmers.

stem: The heavy chemical-intensive farming of the Green Revolution has raised concerns about the __________ of agriculture, prompting a shift toward more sustainable methods.
solution: The heavy, chemical-intensive farming introduced by the Green Revolution (with its large use of chemical fertilisers, pesticides, and water for the HYV crops) has raised serious concerns about the sustainability of agriculture — that is, whether this kind of farming can be continued in the long run without degrading the environment and the resource base. The problems include: the degradation and loss of fertility of the soil (from overuse of chemicals), the depletion and pollution of water (over-extraction of groundwater, and chemical contamination), the loss of biodiversity, and harm to human health. These concerns have prompted a shift toward more sustainable agriculture — methods (like organic farming, integrated pest management, and better water and soil management) that maintain productivity while conserving the environment and resources for the future. Understanding the sustainability concern (and the shift toward sustainable farming) is a prelims-relevant point. Chemical-intensive Green Revolution farming raised concerns about agriculture's sustainability, prompting a shift toward sustainable methods like organic farming.

stem: Sustainable agriculture aims to:
options: meet the food/farming needs of the present without degrading the environment or harming the ability of future generations to farm (conserving soil, water, and ecology)
solution: Sustainable agriculture aims to meet the food and farming needs of the present generation without degrading the environment or depleting the natural resources — so that the land, soil, water, and ecology are conserved and future generations too can continue to farm productively. It seeks to combine reasonable productivity with the long-term health of the environment and resource base — by using methods that conserve and improve the soil (avoiding erosion and chemical degradation), use water efficiently, maintain biodiversity, and reduce pollution and chemical use (e.g., organic farming, crop rotation, integrated pest management, efficient irrigation). It is the opposite of the short-sighted, resource-degrading farming that maximises output at the cost of the future. This idea of sustainability applies the concept of 'sustainable development' to agriculture. Understanding sustainable agriculture is a prelims-relevant point. Sustainable agriculture meets present farming needs without degrading the environment or harming future generations' ability to farm.

stem: Information technology (IT) can aid rural development by:
options: giving farmers access to information (on weather, prices, best practices, and government schemes) and improving services, education, and marketing in rural areas
solution: Information technology (IT) — computers, mobile phones, the internet — can aid rural development in many ways: it can give farmers timely access to information — on the weather (forecasts), market prices (so they can decide when and where to sell, and not be cheated by traders), best farming practices and new technologies, and government schemes and services — helping them make better decisions and get better prices; it can improve the delivery of services (like banking, health, and government services) to rural areas; and it can support rural education, e-marketing (like e-NAM), and even create IT-related rural employment. So IT is a valuable tool for empowering farmers and modernising and developing the rural areas. Understanding the role of IT in rural development is a prelims-relevant point. IT aids rural development by giving farmers access to information (weather, prices, practices, schemes) and improving rural services, education, and marketing.

stem: The problem of 'distress sale' occurs when a poor farmer is forced to sell his produce __________, usually right after the harvest.
options: immediately and at a low price (because he needs cash urgently and lacks storage/holding capacity)
solution: A 'distress sale' occurs when a poor/small farmer is forced to sell his produce immediately after the harvest and at a low price — because he urgently needs cash (e.g., to repay loans to moneylenders/traders, and to meet his family's expenses) and because he lacks the facilities to hold onto the produce (no storage/warehousing of his own, and no capacity to wait for a better price). Right after the harvest, prices are usually low (because everyone is selling at once), and the farmer, unable to wait or store, must sell at these low prices — often to the very trader/moneylender he owes money to, at unfavourable terms. This distress sale means the farmer gets a poor price and remains poor. Providing storage/warehousing, credit, and a Minimum Support Price helps farmers avoid distress sales. Understanding distress sale is a prelims-relevant point. A 'distress sale' is when a poor farmer is forced to sell his produce immediately and at a low price, needing cash and lacking storage.

stem: The problem of DISGUISED unemployment (surplus labour) in rural agriculture makes __________ especially important.
options: creating non-farm employment and diversification (to productively absorb the surplus labour)
solution: The problem of disguised unemployment (surplus/redundant labour) in rural agriculture — where many more people are engaged in farming than are actually needed (so their marginal contribution to output is little or nothing) — makes the creation of non-farm employment and the diversification of the rural economy especially important. Since agriculture is overcrowded with surplus labour, the extra workers need to be moved into productive alternative employment — in allied activities (dairy, fisheries, horticulture) and non-farm work (agro-processing, small industries, services, etc.) — so that they can be productively employed and earn incomes, and the pressure on agriculture is reduced. So tackling rural disguised unemployment requires generating jobs outside crop agriculture (diversification and non-farm employment). Understanding this link (disguised unemployment → need for diversification/non-farm jobs) is a prelims point. Disguised unemployment in agriculture makes creating non-farm employment and diversification important, to productively absorb the surplus labour.

stem: Women play a major role in Indian agriculture (and rural work), yet they often face disadvantages such as:
options: lack of ownership of land, lower wages, and limited access to credit and resources
solution: Women play a major (and often underrecognised) role in Indian agriculture and rural work — they do a large share of the farm labour (sowing, weeding, harvesting, and much of the work in allied activities like dairying), besides household work. Yet they often face serious disadvantages: they usually lack ownership of land (land is typically owned by men), so they have little control over resources; they are often paid lower wages than men for the same work; and they have limited access to credit, inputs, technology, training, and decision-making. Empowering rural women — through land rights, education, self-help groups/micro-credit, and better access to resources — is important both for their well-being (equity) and for rural development (as women's empowerment strongly benefits families and the economy). Understanding the role and disadvantages of women in rural agriculture is a prelims-relevant point. Women play a major role in Indian agriculture but face disadvantages like lack of land ownership, lower wages, and limited access to credit and resources.

stem: The linking of Self-Help Groups (SHGs) to banks (the 'SHG-Bank Linkage' programme, promoted by NABARD) helps by:
options: channeling bank credit to the poor (through their SHGs), and building their savings and creditworthiness
solution: The 'SHG-Bank Linkage' programme (pioneered and promoted by NABARD) links the Self-Help Groups (SHGs) of the poor to the formal banks. Under it, once an SHG has functioned well for some time (its members regularly saving and internally lending), the bank opens an account for the group and lends money to the SHG (which the group then on-lends to its members). This helps by: channeling formal bank credit to the poor — who could not individually get bank loans (lacking collateral) — through their group (the group's discipline and mutual guarantee serving in place of collateral); and building the members' savings habit, creditworthiness, and empowerment. It is a very successful model of taking micro-credit to the rural poor. Understanding the SHG-Bank Linkage (NABARD) is a prelims-relevant point. The SHG-Bank Linkage programme (NABARD) channels bank credit to the poor through their Self-Help Groups, building their savings and creditworthiness.

stem: Agro-processing and food-processing industries (like making jam, juice, dairy products, and packaged foods) help rural development by:
options: adding value to farm produce, reducing wastage, and creating non-farm employment and income in rural areas
solution: Agro-processing and food-processing industries — which process the raw farm produce into value-added products (e.g., turning fruits into jam and juice, milk into butter/cheese, grains into flour and packaged foods, etc.) — help rural development in several ways: they add value to the farm produce (so farmers/the rural economy earn more from the same produce); they reduce the wastage of perishable produce (by processing and preserving it); they create additional non-farm employment and income in the rural areas (in the processing units); and they widen the market for farm produce. So developing agro-/food-processing is an important way to diversify and strengthen the rural economy and raise rural incomes. Understanding the role of agro-processing in rural development is a prelims-relevant point. Agro-/food-processing industries add value to farm produce, reduce wastage, and create non-farm rural employment and income.

stem: The White Revolution's success was based on the 'Anand pattern' of dairy cooperatives, pioneered by __________ (the cooperative in Gujarat).
solution: The White Revolution's success was based on the 'Anand pattern' of dairy cooperatives, pioneered by Amul (the Anand Milk Union Limited) — the milk cooperative based in Anand, in the Kaira/Kheda district of Gujarat. In this cooperative model, the milk of a large number of small rural milk producers is collected through village-level cooperatives, then processed and marketed by the union — cutting out middlemen and ensuring that the producers (the farmers, often small and poor, and women) get a fair, stable price and control. This Amul/Anand pattern was replicated across the country under Operation Flood, making India the world's largest milk producer and transforming rural incomes. Understanding the Amul/Anand pattern is a prelims-relevant point. The White Revolution was based on the 'Anand pattern' of dairy cooperatives, pioneered by Amul in Gujarat.

stem: A major problem with relying on the traditional moneylender for credit was that the loans were often taken for __________, trapping the farmer in a cycle of debt.
options: consumption/unproductive purposes (like weddings, festivals, and daily needs), on which no income was earned to repay
solution: A major problem with relying on the traditional moneylender for credit was that a large part of the loans taken were for consumption and unproductive purposes — such as weddings, festivals, religious ceremonies, funerals, illness, and daily consumption needs — rather than for productive investment in farming. Since these consumption loans did not generate any income (unlike a productive investment that yields a return), the farmer had no way to earn the money to repay them; and with the very high interest charged by the moneylenders, the debt kept mounting, trapping the farmer in a perpetual cycle of debt (often ending in the loss of his land). This is one reason cheap, purposeful institutional credit (for productive uses) was so needed. Understanding this problem (consumption loans → debt trap) is a prelims point. Loans from moneylenders were often taken for consumption/unproductive purposes, on which no income was earned to repay — trapping farmers in debt.

stem: Poor rural infrastructure (roads, electricity, irrigation, storage, banking) holds back rural development because it:
options: limits farmers' access to markets, inputs, credit, and modern methods — lowering productivity and incomes
solution: Poor rural infrastructure — inadequate roads, electricity, irrigation, storage/warehousing, banking, communications, and markets — holds back rural development because it limits the farmers' and rural people's access to the things they need to prosper: without good roads, farmers cannot easily reach markets (to sell produce and buy inputs), and are cut off from towns and services; without electricity and assured irrigation, they cannot use modern methods and their productivity is low and rain-dependent; without storage, they suffer distress sales; without banking, they cannot get credit or save. All this lowers their productivity, incomes, and opportunities. So developing rural infrastructure is essential to enable and support all the other aspects of rural development. Understanding how poor infrastructure holds back rural development is a prelims point. Poor rural infrastructure limits farmers' access to markets, inputs, credit, and modern methods, lowering productivity and incomes.

stem: Although agriculture's share in India's GDP has fallen over the years, it still __________, which is why rural/agricultural development remains vital.
options: employs a very large share of the workforce (a large part of the population still depends on it)
solution: Although the share of agriculture in India's GDP (national income) has fallen over the decades (as industry and services have grown), agriculture still employs a very large share of the workforce — a large part of India's population continues to depend on agriculture (and the rural economy) for its livelihood. This mismatch (a small and falling share of GDP but a large share of employment) means that a huge number of people are dependent on a sector of relatively low productivity and income — which is precisely why rural and agricultural development (raising farm productivity and incomes, and creating non-farm rural jobs) remains vital for improving the lives of this large section of the population and for reducing poverty. Understanding this (agriculture's falling GDP share but large employment share) is a prelims point. Agriculture's GDP share has fallen, but it still employs a very large share of the workforce, so rural/agricultural development remains vital.

stem: Providing farmers with better access to __________ (like weather forecasts, prices, and new techniques) through agricultural extension and IT improves their farming decisions.
solution: Providing farmers with better access to information and knowledge — such as weather forecasts, current and expected market prices, new and better farming techniques and technologies, improved seeds and inputs, pest/disease management, and government schemes — through agricultural extension services (like the Krishi Vigyan Kendras, which spread know-how to farmers) and through modern IT (mobile phones, the internet, farmer information systems) — improves the farmers' decision-making (about what and when to grow, how to grow it better, and when and where to sell). Better-informed farmers can raise their productivity, reduce their risks and losses, and get better prices — so information/knowledge is a valuable input for rural development. Understanding the role of information/knowledge (extension, IT) for farmers is a prelims-relevant point. Better access to information and knowledge (weather, prices, techniques) through extension and IT improves farmers' decisions.

stem: The institutions that transfer agricultural technology and knowledge to farmers at the district level (through training and demonstration) are the:
solution: The Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) — meaning 'Farm Science Centres' — are the institutions (at the district level) that transfer agricultural technology, scientific knowledge, and modern farming practices to the farmers, through training, demonstrations (showing new methods on the ground), and advice. They act as a bridge between the agricultural research institutions/universities and the farmers (agricultural 'extension'), helping farmers to adopt improved seeds, techniques, and technologies, and thus to raise their productivity. KVKs are an important part of the agricultural extension system supporting rural development. Understanding the KVKs (farm science centres for extension) is a prelims-relevant point. Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) are district-level institutions that transfer agricultural technology and knowledge to farmers through training and demonstration.

stem: The overall need for rural development, poverty alleviation, and diversification arises because much of rural India still suffers from:
options: poverty, unemployment/underemployment, low productivity, and inadequate infrastructure and services
solution: The overall need for rural development (and its various measures — credit, marketing, diversification, employment programmes, infrastructure, etc.) arises because much of rural India still suffers from serious problems: widespread poverty; unemployment and underemployment (including disguised unemployment and seasonal joblessness); low agricultural productivity and low incomes; the exploitation of small farmers (in credit and marketing); and inadequate infrastructure (roads, power, irrigation, storage) and social services (education, health, sanitation). These conditions keep a large part of the rural population poor and backward. Rural development aims precisely to address these problems — to raise rural productivity, incomes, employment, and living standards and to reduce poverty. Understanding the problems that necessitate rural development is a prelims point. Rural development is needed because much of rural India still suffers from poverty, unemployment, low productivity, and inadequate infrastructure and services.

stem: Assertion (A): Diversification into allied and non-farm activities is important for rural development. Reason (R): Crop agriculture alone cannot provide enough income and employment for the growing rural population, so alternative sources are needed. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that diversification into allied activities (dairy, fisheries, horticulture) and non-farm activities (agro-processing, services, small industries) is important for rural development. And the reason is (R) that crop agriculture alone cannot provide enough income and employment for the large and growing rural population — the land is limited and overcrowded (with surplus/disguised-unemployed labour), incomes from a single crop are low and risky, and much labour is idle in the off-season — so alternative and additional sources of income and employment are needed. Diversification provides exactly these alternative sources, absorbing the surplus labour and raising and stabilising rural incomes. So R correctly explains why diversification is important (A). Understanding this reasoning is a prelims point. Diversification is important because crop agriculture alone can't provide enough income and employment for the growing rural population, so alternatives are needed.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Rural Development' is that:
options: Since most Indians live in villages and depend on agriculture, the all-round development of the rural areas — through adequate credit and better marketing, the diversification of agriculture into allied and non-farm activities, sustainable (organic) farming, cooperatives, employment programmes, and improved infrastructure and human resources — is essential to raise rural incomes and living standards and to reduce poverty
solution: The chapter conveys that, since a very large proportion of India's population lives in the villages and depends on agriculture, the all-round development of the rural areas is essential for India's overall development and for reducing poverty. It examines the key areas and measures needed for rural development: providing adequate, timely, and cheap institutional credit to farmers (through cooperatives, the nationalisation of banks, NABARD, and micro-credit/Self-Help Groups) to free them from exploitative moneylenders and enable them to invest in farming; improving agricultural marketing (through regulated markets/mandis, warehousing, the Minimum Support Price, and cooperative marketing) so that farmers get a fair price and are not exploited by the many middlemen; promoting the diversification of agriculture — into a wider range of crops and, especially, into allied activities (animal husbandry/dairying — as in the White Revolution, fisheries, horticulture) and non-farm employment — to provide additional incomes and reduce dependence on a single crop; encouraging sustainable and organic farming (to protect the environment and produce healthy food); using the cooperative model (as in dairy — Amul, and in credit and marketing) to empower small rural producers; and implementing employment and poverty-alleviation programmes (like MGNREGA, which guarantees rural wage employment) and improving rural infrastructure (roads, electricity, water, banking) and human resources (education, health). Through such measures, the incomes, employment, and living standards of the rural people can be raised and rural poverty reduced. Understanding what rural development means and the range of measures needed to achieve it is the central concern of this chapter. Rural development — through better credit and marketing, agricultural diversification, sustainable farming, cooperatives, employment programmes, and improved infrastructure — is essential to raise rural incomes and living standards and reduce poverty, since most Indians live in villages.
